amendments.rule: Rule 53 decides a supplied verb by what is left in the clause to carry it, and that test does not turn on the verb being a copula. Where a verbless Greek clause has a prepositional predicate and the ASV supplies a **lexical** verb, the preposition carries it exactly as it carries a supplied *is* or *are*: `τὴν παρὰ τοῦ μόνου θεοῦ` → *that cometh from the only God* gives *cometh from* to `παρά`, as `τὰ παρ᾿ ὑμῶν` → *the things that came from you* gives *came from* to `παρ᾿`, and `ἵνα ἡμεῖς εἰς τὰ ἔθνη` → *that we should go unto the Gentiles* gives a bare *we* to the pronoun and *should go unto* to `εἰς`. An expressed subject does not change this, as `εἴ τις εἰς αἰχμαλωσίαν` → *If any man is for captivity* gives *any man* to `τις` and *is for* to `εἰς`; and rule 17 heads such a unit on the word realizing the preposition, not on the supplied verb. Rule 56 is the contrast and it is the narrow one: it gives the supplied verb to the subject only where the clause expresses no predicate at all, so that the subject is the sole token left to carry it. A prepositional phrase standing in the clause is such a predicate, and the recurring failure is reading the supplied verb off the English word order because the ASV writes it next to the subject. This rule reaches only a supplied verb that the standing prepositional phrase is the **predicate of**, and the test is which way the predication runs. Where the ASV instead supplies a **whole predicate of its own** — a lexical verb together with its own subject and complement — and the standing preposition is that supplied verb's **adjunct**, whose own English the ASV has already written in full, the supplied words answer to no token at all and are their own `added` unit under rule 5, the preposition keeping only the word written for it. `εἴτε διακονίαν, ἐν τῇ διακονίᾳ` → *or ministry, let us give ourselves to our ministry* marks *let us give ourselves* `added` and leaves `ἐν` a bare *to*, as `ὁ μεταδιδοὺς ἐν ἁπλότητι` → *he that giveth, let him do it with liberality* and `εἴτε προφητείαν κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν τῆς πίστεως` → *whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of our faith* do. An elliptical list is where this arises, the Greek writing only the arguments of a predicate it never wrote; and the noun of such an item is ordinarily spent on its own English already, so rule 103's reasoning reaches the same answer from the other side. A preposition whose English the ASV has written in full is not a word a supplied predicate can be a helper on, rule 27 forbidding a helper to be split from what licenses it and nothing here licensing this one. Rule 11 does not decide it either way: the ASV italicizes such a predicate only sometimes, and where it does the italics corroborate rather than license. Rules 63, 68, 75 and 96 are untouched, each of them naming a standing token that the supplied verb predicates of, and so is rule 53, whose supplied copula or auxiliary still folds onto an expressed predicate adjective, as `Ἡ ἀγάπη ἀνυπόκριτος` → *Let love be without hypocrisy* gives *Let ... be* to the adjective.
amendments.why: ROM.12 is the case rule 62 had not considered: 12.18's `τὸ ἐξ ὑμῶν` → *as much as in you lieth* folds a supplied lexical verb onto ἐξ, while 12.6, 12.7 and 12.8 each have a preposition standing in a verbless clause and must mark the ASV's whole supplied imperative predicate `added`. Left as it stands, rule 62's sentence 'Where a verbless Greek clause has a prepositional predicate and the ASV supplies a lexical verb, the preposition carries it' reads as licensing `ἐν` → *let us give ourselves to*, headed on *to* — a fold the chapter had to refuse three times. The qualification is returned as an amendment rather than a new rule because the over-broad sentence is inside rule 62 itself and a cross-reference would leave it standing for whoever reads it first. Nothing in the corpus contradicts it: rule 62's own examples are all cases where the prepositional phrase is what the supplied verb predicates of, and rule 103 already establishes `added` for supplied lexical verbs no token licenses (REV.14.14, 2JN.1.12). The added clause changes no existing unit.

conventions: The charismata list supplies an English imperative predicate for three of its items, and all three are `added` whole: ROM.12.6 let us prophesy, ROM.12.7 let us give ourselves, ROM.12.8 let him do it. The prepositional phrase standing in each clause (κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν, ἐν τῇ διακονίᾳ, ἐν ἁπλότητι) already has its own complete English and is the supplied verb's adjunct rather than the predicate it predicates of, so rule 62 does not reach it, and the noun of each item is spent on its own English (rule 103). The contrasts inside this chapter are ROM.12.9, where the supplied Let ... be folds onto the expressed predicate adjective ἀνυπόκριτος under rule 53, and ROM.12.18 and ROM.12.19, where the supplied lieth and belongeth fold onto ἐξ ὑμῶν and Ἐμοί because those are what the supplied verb predicates of (rules 62, 63).

φρονέω and its compounds are headed by rule 91's operational test throughout. The head is mind wherever the ASV writes a mind-frame — ROM.12.16 Be of the same mind and Set your mind on, which match COL.3.2 and PHP.2.2 word for word, the corpus heading this lemma on mind, minded, mindest or thought and never on think. ROM.12.3's φρονεῖν -> to think and so to think head on think only because no other word stands in the unit; σωφρονεῖν -> to think soberly heads on soberly, the corpus spending sober and soberly on that stem, as rule 91's own σωφρονήσατε -> be ye of sound mind heads on sound; and ὑπερφρονεῖν heads on think with the preverb realized in more highly under rule 106.

report: Read all 31 candidate lemma groups plus the four `added` units end to end. No cross-verse split was found: no construction is analysed two ways with nothing in the source to license the difference, and this pass moves no alignment edge.

The article's 18 treatments are all licensed by the English the ASV wrote. Determiner written vs. not (12.2 τῇ -> by the, 12.13 ταῖς -> to the, 12.19 τῇ -> unto the, against the seven bare datives of 12.10-12.12 left unrepresented under rule 21's determinerless clause). Possessive displaced by a standing genitive pronoun (12.1 τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν, 12.2 τοῦ νοὸς ὑμῶν, 12.20 ὁ ἐχθρός σου) vs. supplied where no pronoun stands, which is rule 20's second arm (12.6 τῆς -> of our, 12.7 τῇ -> our and his, 12.8 τῇ -> his). Substantival article split before a participle (12.3, 12.7, 12.8 four times, 12.14) vs. an anarthrous participle keeping them that whole (12.15), which is rule 32's own test. Article present vs. absent deciding who takes a supplied generic noun: man to the article at 12.3 and things at 12.16 under rule 102, against the anarthrous to no man, to each man and things honorable headed on the quantifier or adjective under rule 17.

Rule 106's case test is applied four times and always the same way: an accusative object keeps the preposition inside the verb (12.13 given to, 12.16 Set your mind on, 12.17 Take thought for), while the dative κολλάομαι governs hands to to the governed substantival article (12.9 τῷ -> to that which). ἐν, εἰς, διά, εἴτε, θεός, πίστις, ἀλλήλων and φρονέω differ only in what the ASV wrote; ἀλλήλων heads on the ἄλλος word in all four units, matching the corpus majority under rule 83, and 12.16's two φρονέω units match COL.3.2 and PHP.2.2 word for word.

The one near-miss is 12.7 against 12.18, invisible to the candidate table because one side is `added`. Both are verbless with a preposition standing and a lexical verb supplied, and they are treated oppositely: 12.18 folds lieth onto ἐξ under rule 62, while 12.6, 12.7 and 12.8 mark let us prophesy, let us give ourselves and let him do it `added` in full and leave κατά and ἐν only their own written English. The difference is source-licensed — in 12.18 the prepositional phrase is what the supplied verb predicates of, in 12.6-12.8 it is that verb's adjunct with its English already complete — so no patch. But rule 62 does not say so, and a reader holding it would fold the italicized predicates, so it is recorded as a convention and returned as an amendment to rule 62.

BSB: none of the six disagreements is a genuine error. 12.1 τήν and 12.2 τοῦ are rule 20 displacements (which is rides with the predicate noun under rule 92, of the with the noun); 12.2 τό is a second attributive article under rule 23; 12.11 τῇ and τῷ are rule 21's determinerless clause, which is the documented convention difference the report itself names. No accepted edge was changed to move the 97.7% figure.

The sixth, 12.3 ὅ, is a genuinely divided call the verse note did not record. The ASV writes than he ought to think with no word between than and he, so the relative is unrepresented under rule 23; but the pair παρ᾽ ὅ maps to the single English word than, which is rule 94's precondition, and joining it as one aligned unit on the model of rule 50's ἕως ἄν -> till is defensible. Rule 16 wants that competing reading in the note, so ROM.12.3 is returned as a note-only patch: the same 31 units, same heads, same edges, one note and one review note extended.

Two conventions recorded (the supplied-predicate judgment of 12.6-12.8 and its 12.9/12.18/12.19 contrast, and the φρονέω head family). One amendment, to rule 62. No corpus request: the two hedged heads that a lemma query could settle — φιλαδελφία -> love of the brethren at 12.10 and προσκαρτερέω -> continuing stedfastly at 12.12 — occur once each, carry rule 16 notes naming the alternative, and would not change any cross-verse judgment, so the single evidence round is left unspent.
